Q001023.stem: A trading firm must survive the loss of an entire data center with no data loss for its order database, keep synchronous-replication latency in the low milliseconds, and also tolerate a full Regional outage with a recovery time of under an hour. Which architecture meets all three goals?

choices.text: Synchronous replication across two Regions, since Regions are designed for low-latency interconnection
Synchronous replication across AZs, plus async replication to a second Region
Multiple instances in one AZ on separate racks, plus nightly snapshots copied to a second Region
Asynchronous replication across AZs, plus synchronous replication to a second Region for zero data loss

Q001023.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Availability Zones in a Region are physically separate (independent power, cooling, and networking) but connected with low-latency private links, which makes synchronous replication practical, so losing one data center or AZ loses no data. Regions are far apart, so replication between them is normally asynchronous. That meets an RTO under an hour for a Regional failure, accepting a small RPO.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synchronous across Regions: inter-Region distance adds latency far above low milliseconds, which would slow every write.
• Racks in one AZ: an AZ-level event takes all of them down, and nightly snapshots give a large RPO.
• Async within the Region, sync across Regions: backwards. It risks data loss for an AZ failure and adds high latency for the cross-Region path.

Key takeaway: AZs are for synchronous, low-latency high availability. Regions are for disaster recovery, usually with asynchronous replication.

Q001034.stem: Security wants to block DNS resolution of malicious and newly registered domains from 300 VPCs across 60 accounts, using AWS-managed threat lists, with logs of blocked queries and the ability to add company-specific domains. New VPCs must be covered automatically. What should the solutions architect implement?

choices.text: DNS Firewall managed and custom lists via Firewall Manager, with query logs
GuardDuty DNS findings with EventBridge rules that add the offending IPs to security groups
Network ACLs on every subnet that deny outbound UDP and TCP 53 except to approved resolvers
AWS Network Firewall in each VPC with stateful domain rules

Q001034.explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall filters queries at the VPC Resolver, including AWS managed domain lists for malware and newly registered domains, plus custom block and allow lists. Firewall Manager applies DNS Firewall policies across accounts and automatically to new VPCs in scope, and Resolver query logging records what was blocked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Network Firewall per VPC: can filter domains in traffic, but it's costly per VPC and doesn't use the managed DNS threat lists at the resolver. It's also more to run.
• NACLs on port 53: can't see domain names at all, and would break DNS to the VPC resolver.
• GuardDuty with SG updates: detective and after the fact. Blocking IPs doesn't stop resolution of new malicious domains.

Key takeaway: domain-level DNS blocking at scale → DNS Firewall with Firewall Manager.

Q001038.stem: An engineer must block a single abusive IP range from reaching web servers in a public subnet while still allowing everyone else on 443. Responses to legitimate clients must keep working. The web servers' security group already allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. What is the correct change?

choices.text: Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 rule from the security group and add allow rules for every other address range
Add a NACL outbound DENY for the range, since NACLs are stateful and will also block inbound
A lower-numbered NACL inbound DENY for the range, keeping ephemeral outbound
Add a DENY rule for the IP range to the web servers' security group above the existing allow rule

Q001038.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups are stateful and allow-only: they can't express 'everyone except X'. Network ACLs are stateless, support DENY, and evaluate rules in ascending number order, so a lower-numbered DENY for the abusive range takes effect before the broader ALLOW 443. Because NACLs are stateless, outbound rules must still allow ephemeral ports so responses reach legitimate clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG deny rule: security groups do not support deny rules.
• Allow-listing everyone else: impractical, and it hits the security group rule limits.
• Outbound NACL deny as if stateful: NACLs are stateless. An outbound rule does not block inbound requests, and it would only break responses.

Key takeaway: deny a specific range → NACL (ordered, stateless); allow-by-reference and stateful → security group.

Q001040.stem: A company must continuously detect CVEs in 3,000 EC2 instances and ECR images across 40 accounts, rescan automatically when new CVEs are published, prioritize by network exposure, and avoid managing separate scanner agents. Most instances already run the SSM Agent. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector org-wide via a delegated administrator
AWS Config rules checking installed package versions, with findings aggregated in Security Hub
A third-party scanner AMI in each account, launched weekly by EventBridge to scan instances
GuardDuty Malware Protection

Q001040.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector continuously scans EC2 (using the SSM Agent, with no separate agent to manage) and ECR images, and automatically rescans when new CVEs appear. Its risk score factors in network reachability, and a delegated administrator enables and views it across the organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config package-version rules: Config tracks configuration and isn't a CVE database, so you'd build the vulnerability logic yourself.
• Weekly third-party scanner: not continuous, adds infrastructure, and misses newly published CVEs between runs.
• GuardDuty Malware Protection plus basic scanning: malware isn't CVEs, and basic ECR scanning runs only at push without continuous rescans.

Key takeaway: continuous CVE management for EC2, ECR, and Lambda → Amazon Inspector, org-wide via delegated admin.

Q001058.stem: In a Control Tower landing zone, an auditor asks how the company prevents workload administrators from deleting CloudTrail logs that record their own actions. Which design BEST explains this?

choices.text: A dedicated Log Archive account, with preventive controls on members
IAM Identity Center permission sets exclude cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
Each workload account keeps its own trail in a local bucket protected by MFA Delete
The management account stores all logs so workload administrators can't sign in to it

Q001058.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower separates duties with dedicated accounts. The Log Archive account centrally stores organization CloudTrail and Config logs, and mandatory preventive controls (SCPs) stop member accounts from disabling or changing the logging setup. Workload administrators have no rights in the Log Archive account, so they can't erase evidence of their own actions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local trails with MFA Delete: the same account admins who are being audited own the bucket and can change settings.
• Logs in the management account: best practice is to keep the management account minimal. Log storage belongs in a separate, locked-down account.
• Removing DeleteTrail from permission sets: doesn't stop other ways to disable logging, such as deleting the bucket, and can be changed by whoever administers Identity Center.

Key takeaway: put audit evidence in a different account from the people being audited, and enforce it with preventive controls.

Q001064.stem: Application teams request new AWS accounts weekly. Each account must arrive with standard guardrails, a baseline VPC, security tooling, and team-specific customizations kept in Terraform, with no manual steps by the platform team. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A Config aggregator that detects new accounts and reports missing baseline resources
Control Tower Account Factory for Terraform (AFT), with account requests and customizations in Git
IAM Identity Center permission sets that grant each team rights to build its own baseline
Organizations CreateAccount from a script, followed by a manual checklist for guardrails and networking

Q001064.explanation:
Why this is correct:
AFT extends Control Tower Account Factory with a GitOps workflow. Account requests are committed as Terraform, the account is vended and enrolled with Control Tower guardrails, and global and account-specific customizations (baseline VPC, security tools) are applied automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Script plus checklist: the manual steps are exactly what the platform team wants to eliminate, and they invite drift.
• Permission sets for self-build: gives access, not a consistent baseline. Each team would build it differently.
• Config aggregator: detects missing pieces after the fact. It doesn't provision anything.

Key takeaway: automated, customized account vending → Account Factory; Terraform-based customizations → AFT.

Q001066.stem: Finance wants to analyze two years of spend by service and cost-center tag, receive an alert when the forecast predicts a monthly overrun, and have a non-production account's EC2 instances stopped automatically if its budget is exceeded. Which combination meets all requirements?

choices.text: Cost Explorer for trends; Budgets with forecast alerts and a stop action
Trusted Advisor cost checks for trends, and Budgets alerts that email the team to stop instances
Pricing Calculator for trends, and Cost Anomaly Detection to stop instances when the budget is exceeded
CloudWatch billing alarms for forecasts, and Cost Explorer to stop instances when spend is exceeded

Q001066.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost Explorer analyzes historical spend, grouped by service or cost allocation tag. AWS Budgets supports forecast-based alerts and budget actions, which can apply IAM or SCP policies or stop specific EC2 or RDS instances when a threshold is crossed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Billing alarms and Cost Explorer: billing alarms track estimated charges, not forecasts, and Cost Explorer cannot act on resources.
• Pricing Calculator and Anomaly Detection: the Pricing Calculator estimates planned architectures, not history. Anomaly Detection flags unusual spend but has no stop action.
• Trusted Advisor with email: Trusted Advisor isn't a trend tool, and email means manual action.

Key takeaway: history → Cost Explorer; thresholds, forecasts, and automated responses → Budgets and budget actions.

Q001067.stem: A company wants weekly, organization-wide reports on security groups open to the internet, service quota usage near limits, idle load balancers, and underused EBS volumes, delivered to a central team, using AWS Business Support. Which service provides these checks directly?

choices.text: AWS Compute Optimizer with enhanced infrastructure metrics
AWS Config with managed rules for each check
AWS Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations
AWS Trusted Advisor with organizational view

Q001067.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor checks span security (for example, open security group ports), service limits, fault tolerance, performance, and cost (idle load balancers, underutilized EBS). With Business Support or higher the full set of checks is available, and organizational view aggregates results across accounts for a central team.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compute Optimizer: rightsizing recommendations for compute and EBS only. No security group or quota checks.
• Config managed rules: could cover some configuration checks, but not quota usage or idle-resource cost checks without significant custom work.
• Cost Explorer rightsizing: EC2 cost recommendations only.

Key takeaway: broad best-practice checks across security, cost, limits, and resilience → Trusted Advisor. Deep rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.

Q001069.stem: A company has 900 buckets across 70 accounts. It wants organization-wide metrics on storage growth, the share of noncurrent versions, and incomplete multipart uploads, plus recommendations to cut cost, exported daily for analysis. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: CloudWatch storage metrics per bucket, combined in a cross-account dashboard
Trusted Advisor S3 checks with organizational view
S3 Storage Lens organization dashboard with daily export
S3 Inventory in every bucket, queried with Athena and a custom QuickSight dashboard

Q001069.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storage Lens aggregates usage and activity metrics across accounts and Regions. It highlights cost-saving opportunities such as noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads, provides recommendations, and can export metrics daily to S3 for further analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Inventory plus Athena: possible, but you'd build the organization-wide aggregation, metrics, and recommendations yourself for 900 buckets.
• CloudWatch storage metrics: basic size and object counts, with no insight into noncurrent versions or incomplete uploads and no recommendations.
• Trusted Advisor: a few S3 checks (mainly permissions and versioning), not organization-wide storage analytics.

Key takeaway: organization-wide S3 usage visibility and optimization → S3 Storage Lens.

Q001071.stem: Before approving a migration, leadership wants a shareable monthly cost estimate for a planned three-tier application, comparing On-Demand with a 3-year Savings Plan, two instance families, gp3 versus io2 storage, and 20 TB of monthly data transfer out. Which tool fits BEST?

choices.text: Cost Explorer forecasts based on the current account's spending history
AWS Pricing Calculator with grouped, shared estimates
Compute Optimizer recommendations for the planned instance families
AWS Budgets with a forecast

Q001071.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Pricing Calculator models architectures that don't exist yet. You configure services, pricing models (On-Demand versus Savings Plans), storage types, and data transfer, group them, and share or export the estimate for approval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer forecasts: based on past spending. It knows nothing about an application that hasn't been deployed.
• Compute Optimizer: analyzes running resources' utilization, so there's nothing to analyze yet.
• Budgets: tracks and forecasts actual spend against thresholds after deployment.

Key takeaway: before deployment → Pricing Calculator; after deployment → Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Compute Optimizer.

Q001082.stem: An ECS service needs a database password injected at container start. The password must rotate every 30 days without redeploying tasks, each access must be auditable, and only this service's task role may read it. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: A rotating Secrets Manager secret referenced in the task definition
An environment variable in the task definition
A Parameter Store Standard parameter referenced in the task definition, rotated by a scheduled Lambda
An SSE-S3 encrypted S3 object downloaded by the container at startup with the task role

Q001082.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secrets Manager provides managed rotation for supported databases. ECS task definitions can reference a secret in the secrets section, so the value is injected at container start. Every GetSecretValue call is logged in CloudTrail, and resource and IAM policies can restrict access to the specific role that retrieves it. After rotation, newly started tasks receive the new value without a task definition change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store with custom rotation: no managed rotation, so you'd write and maintain the rotation and database-update logic yourself.
• S3 object: not a secrets store. There's no rotation, and anyone with bucket access can read it.
• Plain environment variable: visible in the task definition, and rotation requires a redeploy, which violates the requirement.

Key takeaway: rotating credentials with audit → Secrets Manager. Static configuration → Parameter Store.

Q001089.stem: An internal reporting app (EC2, RDS for PostgreSQL, and S3 files) can tolerate an 8-hour RTO and a 24-hour RPO after a Regional disaster. The budget allows almost no standing cost in the DR Region, but recovery must be repeatable. Which strategy fits BEST?

choices.text: Pilot light: a continuously replicated RDS replica in the DR Region, with the app tier built on failover
Warm standby: a scaled-down copy of the full stack running in the DR Region at all times
Multi-site active-active across both Regions with Route 53 latency routing
Backup and restore: AWS Backup copies to the DR Region, S3 CRR, and IaC to rebuild the stack on demand

Q001089.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With hours of RTO and a day of RPO, backup and restore is sufficient and cheapest. Cross-Region backup copies of RDS and EC2 volumes and S3 replication protect the data, and infrastructure as code rebuilds the environment consistently when needed, with almost no standing compute cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pilot light: a running cross-Region replica adds continuous cost to meet an RPO the business doesn't need.
• Warm standby: runs compute continuously, far exceeding the budget for this tolerance.
• Active-active: the most expensive option, justified only for near-zero RTO and RPO.

Key takeaway: match the DR strategy to RTO/RPO. Paying for faster recovery than required wastes money, and IaC is what makes backup and restore repeatable.

Q001090.stem: A SaaS app runs in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-northeast-1. Users must reach the Region with the best network performance, traffic must avoid a Region whose application health check fails, and EU users must stay in the EU for compliance. Which Route 53 configuration meets all requirements?

choices.text: Geolocation for Europe, latency records with health checks for others
Weighted routing with equal weights and health checks on each Region's endpoint
Geoproximity routing with bias values tuned so EU users usually reach eu-west-1
Latency-based routing with health checks for all users

Q001090.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compliance requires deterministic placement of EU users, which geolocation provides. Route 53 supports nested policies (for example, with Traffic Flow or alias records to latency sets), so non-EU users get latency-based routing, and health checks remove unhealthy endpoints from answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency-based for everyone: an EU user could be routed outside the EU if another Region measures faster, which violates compliance.
• Geoproximity with bias: routes by distance and bias, so it doesn't guarantee EU users stay in the EU.
• Weighted routing: ignores both user location and network performance.

Key takeaway: hard location rules → geolocation; performance → latency; combine them with nested records and health checks.

Q001092.stem: A production RDS for MySQL database must fail over automatically within about a minute during an AZ outage, the application must keep using the same endpoint, and the team also wants to offload read-only reporting queries to already-provisioned standby capacity. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: A single-AZ instance with a read replica that is promoted manually during outages
A cross-Region read replica, promoted automatically when the primary AZ fails
A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, sending reporting queries to its standby instance
A Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two readable standbys and a reader endpoint

Q001092.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standbys in different AZs. Failover is automatic and typically faster than a Multi-AZ instance deployment, applications keep using the cluster endpoint, and the reader endpoint lets reporting use the standby capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-AZ DB instance: the standby is not readable, so reporting can't use it.
• Read replica promoted manually: failover isn't automatic, and promotion changes the endpoint.
• Cross-Region replica: RDS doesn't automatically promote a cross-Region replica for an AZ failure, and it adds unnecessary cross-Region lag.

Key takeaway: Multi-AZ instance = HA only. Multi-AZ cluster = HA plus readable standbys. Read replicas = read scaling or DR with manual promotion.

Q001097.stem: An RDS for PostgreSQL database holds regulated data. Security requires encryption at rest with a key the company controls and can disable in an emergency, annual key rotation, key-usage logs, and the ability for a DR account to restore snapshots. Which approach meets all requirements?

choices.text: Use the AWS managed key aws/rds, which rotates automatically and can be shared with other accounts
A customer managed KMS key with rotation, shared via its key policy
Require SSL/TLS for all connections and encrypt backups with SSE-S3
Encrypt sensitive columns in the application and leave storage encryption disabled

Q001097.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A customer managed key gives the company control: it can be disabled, rotation can be enabled, and usage is logged in CloudTrail. Snapshots encrypted with a customer managed key can be shared with another account once the key policy grants that account use of the key, which enables DR restores.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed key: rotates automatically, but you can't manage its key policy, so snapshots encrypted with it can't be shared cross-account, and you can't disable it.
• SSL/TLS plus SSE-S3: TLS protects data in transit, not at rest, and RDS storage isn't encrypted with SSE-S3.
• Column encryption only: leaves storage, logs, and backups unencrypted, which misses the at-rest requirement.

Key takeaway: control, disable, share cross-account → customer managed KMS key.

Q001100.stem: An application on EC2 in Account A must read an S3 bucket in Account A and write to a DynamoDB table in Account B. Security forbids long-term credentials on instances and requires least privilege. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: An instance profile role with AdministratorAccess in Account A, and a DynamoDB resource policy granting Account A full access
Access keys for a user in Account B stored in Secrets Manager in Account A and read at startup
An instance profile role in A for S3; the app assumes a scoped role in B (trusting A's role) for DynamoDB
An IAM user with access keys stored in the instance's environment variables, with permissions in both accounts

Q001100.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The instance profile gives the application temporary, automatically rotated credentials for its own-account resources. For the other account, it calls sts:AssumeRole on a role in Account B whose trust policy allows only Account A's instance role, and whose permissions allow only the needed DynamoDB actions on that table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM user keys: long-term credentials on the instance, which is forbidden.
• AdministratorAccess and full access: violates least privilege on both sides.
• Account B user keys in Secrets Manager: still long-term credentials. Storing them in a secret doesn't make them temporary.

Key takeaway: own account → instance profile; other account → AssumeRole into a narrowly scoped, trusted role.

Q001103.stem: A company with 80 accounts in 3 Regions must continuously measure compliance against CIS AWS Foundations and PCI DSS, view one consolidated score per standard, and automatically route new critical findings to a ticketing system. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Artifact reports for CIS and PCI DSS downloaded monthly and reviewed by auditors
Security Hub org-wide with aggregation and EventBridge routing
Trusted Advisor security checks with organizational view and weekly email reports
Amazon Inspector CIS scans on EC2 instances

Q001103.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Hub runs automated checks for standards such as CIS AWS Foundations and PCI DSS and shows a score per standard. A delegated administrator plus cross-Region aggregation gives one organization-wide view, and findings are emitted to EventBridge, where rules can route critical ones to ticketing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Artifact: provides AWS's own compliance reports (for example, AWS's PCI attestation), not checks of your accounts.
• Trusted Advisor: a limited set of security checks, not mapped to CIS or PCI controls, and weekly email isn't continuous routing.
• Inspector CIS scans: assess operating system configuration on instances, not AWS account-level controls across services.

Key takeaway: account-level standards compliance and a findings hub → Security Hub. AWS's own attestations → Artifact.

Q001119.stem: During flash sales, the web tier receives 20x normal orders, and the order-processing tier (EC2, about 2 seconds per order) falls behind and drops requests. Orders must never be lost, customers can receive confirmation by email later, and processing must scale with the backlog. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: Vertically scale the processors to the largest instance type during sales
Scale the processing tier on CPU utilization and add retries in the web tier
Put a Network Load Balancer between the tiers and raise the processors' connection timeouts
Write orders to SQS and scale the processors on queue depth (backlog per instance)

Q001119.explanation:
Why this is correct:
A queue decouples intake from processing. Orders are stored durably in SQS the moment they arrive, so a slow backend no longer causes drops. Scaling the consumers on backlog per instance (queue depth ÷ instances) adds capacity in proportion to the actual work waiting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB and longer timeouts: requests still wait synchronously and are lost when the backend is saturated.
• CPU scaling with retries: CPU lags the real backlog, and retries amplify load during the spike.
• Vertical scaling: has a ceiling, requires downtime to resize, and still drops requests beyond that ceiling.

Key takeaway: when work can be asynchronous, queue it and scale consumers on backlog, not CPU.

Q001127.stem: A company wants a monthly review that finds idle load balancers, underutilized EBS volumes, and unassociated Elastic IPs across 50 accounts, and also gets rightsizing recommendations for EC2 instances based on memory and CPU usage. Which combination fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Budgets for idle resources, and Pricing Calculator for rightsizing
Trusted Advisor cost checks plus Compute Optimizer
Cost Explorer forecasts for idle resources, and Trusted Advisor for memory-based rightsizing
Compute Optimizer for idle load balancers and Elastic IPs, and Budgets for rightsizing

Q001127.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor's cost checks flag idle load balancers, underutilized EBS volumes, and unassociated Elastic IPs, and organizational view covers all accounts. Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization history, including memory when the CloudWatch agent publishes it, to recommend EC2 sizes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets and Pricing Calculator: neither finds idle resources or recommends sizes from utilization.
• Cost Explorer and Trusted Advisor for memory rightsizing: forecasts don't identify idle resources, and Trusted Advisor's checks don't use memory metrics.
• Compute Optimizer for load balancers and EIPs: its scope is compute resources and EBS, not idle load balancers or Elastic IPs.

Key takeaway: waste detection → Trusted Advisor; utilization-based rightsizing → Compute Optimizer.

Q001130.stem: Petabytes of compliance recordings must be kept for 7 years and must not be deleted early by anyone. They are almost never read, and retrieval within 48 hours is acceptable. Recordings land in S3 Standard. Which design is MOST cost-effective while meeting the retention rule?

choices.text: Intelligent-Tiering with the Deep Archive Access tier and a delete-deny SCP
Lifecycle to S3 Standard-IA with Versioning and MFA Delete enabled
Lifecycle to Deep Archive plus Object Lock compliance mode
Lifecycle to Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a bucket policy denying deletes

Q001130.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, and its standard retrieval within 12 hours (bulk within 48) fits the access pattern. Object Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion or retention shortening by any user, including root, until the retention period ends.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flexible Retrieval with a bucket policy: costs more than Deep Archive, and bucket policies can be changed by administrators, so they don't guarantee retention.
• Standard-IA with MFA Delete: far more expensive for petabytes, and MFA Delete can be disabled by the bucket owner.
• Intelligent-Tiering with an SCP: adds per-object monitoring fees for data with a known access pattern, and SCPs can be changed by the management account.

Key takeaway: a known 'never read' pattern → direct lifecycle to Deep Archive; 'no one can delete' → Object Lock compliance mode.

Q001135.stem: On-call engineers receive separate pages for high CPU, high latency, and 5xx errors on the same service, often all at once. The team wants one page only when latency and 5xx errors are both alarming, but wants a warning ticket, not a page, for CPU alone. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: A paging composite alarm on latency AND 5xx
Longer evaluation periods on all three alarms so they fire less often
One alarm on a metric math sum of CPU, latency, and 5xx with a combined threshold
Anomaly detection bands on all three metrics, each paging on-call

Q001135.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Composite alarms evaluate other alarms' states with AND/OR/NOT logic, so paging only happens when customer impact (latency plus errors) is confirmed. The CPU alarm stays useful as a non-paging signal routed to a ticketing topic, and the underlying alarms can suppress their own notifications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Anomaly detection on all three: changes the thresholds but still pages three times.
• Summing unrelated metrics: CPU percent, milliseconds, and error counts have different units, so a combined threshold is meaningless.
• Longer evaluation periods: delays alerts without reducing duplication.

Key takeaway: page on symptoms that matter (combined with composite alarms), and route causes such as CPU to lower-urgency channels.

Q001144.stem: A data lake with 4 PB across 200 buckets in 30 accounts may contain unmasked SSNs and card numbers. The company wants continuous, cost-controlled discovery across all accounts, plus a custom identifier for its internal employee ID format. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Config rules that flag buckets without default encryption as containing PII
Comprehend PII detection in Lambda for every object
Macie automated discovery with a custom data identifier
Daily full Macie classification jobs over every object in all 200 buckets

Q001144.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie is built for discovering sensitive data in S3. Automated sensitive data discovery samples objects continuously across the estate at controlled cost, a delegated administrator manages all member accounts, and custom data identifiers (regex plus keywords) detect company-specific formats such as employee IDs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily full jobs: rescanning 4 PB daily is very expensive and unnecessary for estate-wide visibility.
• Comprehend in Lambda: custom plumbing, it reprocesses the whole backlog, and it has no bucket-level inventory or findings management.
• Config encryption rules: encryption status says nothing about whether PII is present.

Key takeaway: find sensitive data at rest in S3 at scale → Macie (automated discovery plus custom identifiers).

Q001148.stem: An API promises 99.9% monthly availability. The SRE team wants to see the remaining error budget in real time and be alerted when the burn rate predicts exhaustion before month-end, with no custom servers. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A monthly Athena query over CloudTrail logs to count failed API calls
Trusted Advisor availability checks reviewed at the end of each month
Route 53 health checks every 30 seconds
Request-based SLOs with burn-rate alarms

Q001148.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Availability SLOs are best expressed as good requests ÷ total requests. CloudWatch can compute this from ALB metrics (for example, total minus 5xx) with metric math or with Application Signals SLOs, which track error budget and support burn-rate alarms that warn before the budget runs out.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: doesn't measure your API's request success rate.
• CloudTrail: records AWS control-plane API calls, not your application's HTTP requests.
• Health check pings: sample availability from outside with coarse probes and miss partial failures that real users experience.

Key takeaway: request-based SLIs, error budgets, and burn-rate alerts are native CloudWatch capabilities.

Q001151.stem: A session store runs self-managed Redis on EC2. Manual failover after node failures causes minutes of downtime. The team wants Redis compatibility, automatic failover in seconds, and no patching, and would prefer not to size nodes at all. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: ElastiCache Serverless (Redis OSS or Valkey)
DynamoDB with DAX, rewriting the session code to use DynamoDB APIs
A single-node ElastiCache cluster with daily snapshots for recovery
Self-managed Redis Sentinel on three EC2 instances in different AZs

Q001151.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ElastiCache Serverless provides a Redis-compatible (Redis OSS or Valkey) endpoint with no nodes to size or patch. Data is replicated across AZs with automatic failover, which removes the manual failover problem. A node-based replication group with Multi-AZ would also work, but requires sizing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed Sentinel: improves failover but keeps patching and operations on the team.
• DynamoDB with DAX: not Redis-compatible, so it requires a rewrite.
• Single node with snapshots: no failover at all, and restores cause downtime and data loss.

Key takeaway: managed Redis compatibility with HA and no node management → ElastiCache Serverless.

Q001153.stem: An API's average latency is 120 ms and the dashboard looks healthy, yet customers complain. Investigation shows 2% of requests take over 4 seconds. The team wants alerts that reflect customer experience without paging on a single slow request. What should it change?

choices.text: Alarm on the Maximum statistic with one datapoint to catch every slow request
Alarm on p99 with M-of-N datapoints
Alarm on the SampleCount of requests to detect traffic drops
Keep the Average statistic

Q001153.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Averages hide tail latency. A p99 (or p95) statistic shows what the slowest users experience. Requiring M of N datapoints to breach avoids paging on isolated blips while still catching sustained tail degradation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower average threshold: the average stays low when most requests are fast, so the tail problem remains invisible.
• Maximum with one datapoint: pages on any single outlier, causing alert noise.
• SampleCount: measures request volume, not latency.

Key takeaway: alert on percentiles for user experience, and use M-of-N evaluation to control noise.

Q001154.stem: A critical service must stay fully available with no capacity loss if one Availability Zone fails. It needs 12 instances at peak. The team wants to minimize over-provisioning while meeting this goal. Which deployment fits BEST?

choices.text: Two AZs with 6 instances each (12 total), relying on Auto Scaling to replace capacity
Three AZs with 6 instances each (18 total), so any two AZs still provide 12
One AZ with 12 instances in a spread placement group to avoid shared hardware
Two AZs with 12 instances each (24 total), so either AZ alone covers peak

Q001154.explanation:
Why this is correct:
To lose no capacity after an AZ failure, the remaining AZs must carry peak load. With N AZs you need peak ÷ (N−1) per AZ. Three AZs give 12 ÷ 2 = 6 per AZ (18 total, 50% extra). Two AZs would need 12 per AZ (24 total, 100% extra), so three AZs meet the goal with less over-provisioning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two AZs with 6 each: after an AZ failure only 6 remain, a capacity loss until Auto Scaling launches replacements, and an AZ event may constrain those launches.
• Two AZs with 12 each: meets the goal but costs more than the three-AZ design.
• One AZ with spread placement: spread placement protects against rack failure, not an AZ outage.

Key takeaway: static stability across AZs means pre-provisioning so the surviving AZs can handle peak. More AZs means less overhead.

Q001159.stem: Behind an ALB, application processes on some instances hang while the OS stays healthy. The Auto Scaling group uses EC2 status checks only. The team wants hung instances replaced automatically, but not killed during a 5-minute warm-up after launch. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: Set the health check grace period to 0 so failures are detected immediately
Keep EC2 status checks and add a CloudWatch alarm that reboots instances on high CPU
Increase the minimum capacity
ELB health checks with a 5-minute grace period

Q001159.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With the ELB health check type, the Auto Scaling group replaces instances that fail the load balancer's health check. An application-level path (such as /health) catches hung processes that EC2 status checks can't see. The grace period prevents replacing instances that are still warming up.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CPU-based reboot: a hung process may not use high CPU, and rebooting doesn't replace the instance through the group.
• Grace period 0: new instances would be marked unhealthy during warm-up and replaced in a loop.
• More minimum capacity: hung instances still receive traffic and return errors.

Key takeaway: the health check must test what actually fails. For application hangs, use ELB or application health checks with an appropriate grace period.

Q001161.stem: A web tier behind an ALB runs in an Auto Scaling group (min 4, desired 6, max 20) with target tracking on request count per target. At 3 AM one instance fails its health check while traffic is low. What does the group do?

choices.text: Waits for a scale-out event
Does nothing until an operator manually replaces the unhealthy instance
Replaces the failed instance to restore 6
Scales in to 4 instances, since low traffic makes the failed instance unnecessary

Q001161.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Self-healing keeps the running, healthy instance count at the desired capacity: an unhealthy instance is terminated and replaced regardless of load. Elasticity is separate. Scaling policies change the desired capacity itself in response to load. So the group first restores 6 healthy instances, and target tracking may later adjust the desired count within 4 to 20.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Waiting for scale-out: health replacement doesn't depend on scaling policies.
• Scale in because of the failure: a failure doesn't change desired capacity. Only a scaling policy or schedule does.
• Manual replacement: the whole point of health-based replacement is that it's automatic.

Key takeaway: self-healing keeps desired capacity healthy; elasticity changes desired capacity. They are separate mechanisms that work together.

Q001172.stem: A company's heavily customized on-premises CRM is expensive to maintain. The migration plan decommissions it, moves its data into a commercial SaaS CRM bought through AWS Marketplace, and rebuilds two critical customizations as integrations using Lambda. Which migration strategy primarily describes the CRM decision?

choices.text: Retire: decommission the CRM with no replacement
Repurchase: replace the application with a SaaS product
Refactor: re-architect the existing CRM as cloud-native services
Replatform: move the CRM to AWS with a managed database

Q001172.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Repurchase (drop and shop) means moving to a different product, typically SaaS. The existing application is abandoned and its data migrated. Building a few integrations around the new SaaS product doesn't change that the application itself was replaced.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Refactor: re-architects the same application's code. Here the code is thrown away.
• Replatform: keeps the application and makes a few cloud optimizations, such as a managed database.
• Retire: turns off functionality that is no longer needed. Here the CRM function continues in a new product.

Key takeaway: ask what happens to the application. Replaced by a product → repurchase; turned off → retire; code rewritten → refactor.

Q001179.stem: A manufacturing execution system is tightly coupled to plant-floor controllers with millisecond latency needs, and its vendor supports only on-premises installation. The rest of the data center is moving to AWS. The company keeps the system on premises with Direct Connect to AWS and will revisit the decision in 3 years. Which strategy applies to this system?

choices.text: Rehost: lift and shift it to EC2 with Application Migration Service
Retain: keep it on premises for now, with hybrid connectivity
Retire: decommission it and replace it with plant-floor scripts
Relocate: move it to VMware Cloud on AWS unchanged

Q001179.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retain (revisit) keeps an application in its current environment because of constraints such as hardware coupling, latency, or vendor support, often with hybrid connectivity to migrated workloads and a plan to reassess later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Relocate: moves the platform (for example, VMware) to AWS, which is still off premises and conflicts with the controller latency and vendor constraints.
• Rehost: also moves it to AWS, which breaks those same constraints.
• Retire: the system is still needed, so it isn't being decommissioned.

Key takeaway: 'stays where it is for a reason, reassess later' = retain.

Q001184.stem: A company must plan migration waves for 900 VMware VMs. For 50 business-critical servers, it needs running processes and TCP connections between servers to map dependencies; for the rest, inventory and utilization are enough. Guest OS changes on the 850 servers are restricted. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Agentless Collector only, since it also captures process-level network connections
Discovery Agents on all 900 servers so every dependency is captured
A CSV import of server specs into Migration Hub for all 900 servers
Agentless for all VMs, agents on the 50 critical servers

Q001184.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Agentless Collector runs as an appliance in vCenter and gathers VM inventory and performance data without touching guest operating systems, which fits the 850 restricted servers. Discovery Agents installed in the guest OS collect process and network connection data, which is needed for dependency mapping, but only on the 50 servers where they're allowed and valuable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Agents everywhere: violates the guest OS restriction and adds operational effort beyond what's needed.
• Agentless only: doesn't provide process-level connection data for dependency mapping.
• CSV import: static specifications, with no utilization or dependency data.

Key takeaway: agentless = broad inventory and utilization; agent = deep process and network detail. Mix them by server criticality.

Q001193.stem: A team is migrating a Java web app in two weeks. It wants AWS to provision the load balancer, Auto Scaling group, and health monitoring, to deploy new versions with zero downtime and quick rollback, and to keep SSH access to instances for troubleshooting. Containers are out of scope. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Lambda with SnapStart and aliases for rollback
Amazon ECS on Fargate with rolling deployments
EC2 instances configured manually
Elastic Beanstalk with immutable deployments

Q001193.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic Beanstalk provisions and manages the load balancer, Auto Scaling group, and health reporting for a standard Java app while leaving instances accessible. Immutable deployments, or blue/green using an environment CNAME swap, provide zero-downtime releases and fast rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ECS on Fargate: containers are out of scope, and there are no instances to access.
• Lambda: requires re-architecting a traditional web app, which isn't feasible in two weeks and has no server access.
• Manual EC2 with in-place deployments: the team would provision everything itself, and in-place deploys don't give zero downtime or quick rollback.

Key takeaway: fastest managed path for a traditional web app with instance access → Elastic Beanstalk; pick the deployment policy based on the rollback need.

Q001197.stem: After containerizing, a team needs a private image registry shared by 12 accounts. Images must be scanned for CVEs, tags must not be overwritten, images must be replicated to a second Region for DR, and pulls must stay private from workloads in VPCs without internet access. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: A self-hosted registry on EC2 with a public IP and security groups limited to the accounts
Amazon ECR with its governance and private access features
AWS CodeArtifact repositories shared across accounts, with images stored as generic packages
An S3 bucket storing image tarballs, with a bucket policy for the 12 accounts and CRR for DR

Q001197.explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECR meets every requirement natively: repository policies grant cross-account pulls, tag immutability prevents overwrites, enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector) finds CVEs, registry replication copies images to another Region, and interface endpoints for the ECR API and Docker registry plus an S3 gateway endpoint let private subnets pull images without internet access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeArtifact: a package manager repository (npm, Maven, pip), not a container registry for ECS or EKS image pulls.
• S3 tarballs: runtimes can't pull from S3 directly, and there's no scanning or tag management.
• Self-hosted registry with a public IP: an operational burden, it exposes the registry, and it doesn't serve private subnets without extra networking.

Key takeaway: container images → ECR, and turn on its governance features (immutability, scanning, replication, private endpoints).

Q001369.stem: A compliance team must deploy the same versioned set of 30 AWS Config rules with remediation to 50 accounts, including accounts added later, and report one compliance score per account for that set. Which AWS Config feature fits BEST?

choices.text: An organization conformance pack deployed from the Config delegated administrator
Individual Config rules created in each account by a StackSet, with scores calculated in a spreadsheet
Firewall Manager security group policies applied across the organization
A Config aggregator in the audit account that pushes the rules to member accounts

Q001369.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Conformance packs bundle Config rules and remediation actions into one versioned template. Organization conformance packs deploy that bundle to all member accounts, including new ones, and Config reports a compliance score per conformance pack for each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Individual rules via StackSets: they deploy, but the rules aren't managed as a package and there's no native per-pack score.
• Aggregators: collect and display data across accounts. They don't deploy rules.
• Firewall Manager security group policies: manage security groups, not arbitrary compliance rule sets.

Key takeaway: deploy a rule bundle org-wide → organization conformance pack; view results centrally → aggregator.
